en: The Collection for Reviving the Patriarchs by Precious Clouds (with Preface), compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shizhi in Siming.
That which is transmitted cannot exceed the Way; that which can propagate it must rely upon persons. It does not exist because there are persons, nor...
Though the Way remains constant even when it lacks proponents, if there is no one to propagate it, what benefit will the Way bring to living beings?
Only by finding the right person to propagate the Way so that it is not severed can this Way become as manifest as the sun and moon,
providing illumination for all time.
Dharma Master Baoyun (Yitong) was originally of the royal clan of Goryeo; delighting in the Way and weary of the world, he followed the Buddha to undergo tonsure.
He was the first to transmit the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Awakening of Faith*, and the assembly followed him with joy. Upon reaching maturity, he crossed the vast ocean to come to China.

Initially, he visited Yunju and attained realization in the Southern School. Later, he reflected deeply upon the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai and Zhiyi, noting that the scriptures had been separated from them for five dynasties.

With the Dharma reduced to a single thread amidst the chaos, he resolved his will to visit the chamber of Master Jikō at Sōkei-ji and immediately received his transmission. His mastery of the teachings spread in all directions;
subsequently, he vowed to return to his native country to propagate the Dharma. Accordingly, he took up his staff and boarded a ship at Shiming. By chance—

The Prefectural Governor, Prince of Huaihai, Master Qian (Weizhi), inquired about the essentials of the mind and appointed him as his preceptor for the precepts. From then on, both monastics and laypeople turned toward him;

he was earnestly entreated to remain and propagate the Dharma. The Transport Commissioner, Master Gu (Chenghui), donated his residence to establish a temple and commissioned the Master to be its founding patriarch.
As lions and elephants gathered like clouds, he lectured and expounded the teachings for twenty years, after which he entrusted the Great Dharma to [his successor].

Fazhi (Zhipan) paid homage to the Master, who was known as the Venerable of Siming. Fazhi presided over Yanqing Temple for nearly forty years, whereby this Way flourished greatly throughout the world.
Is this not what is meant by saying that it was through obtaining a person capable of transmitting and propagating the teachings that such a result was achieved?
(Zongxiao) Recently, acting upon my long-held aspiration, I have compiled and edited the extant writings of the Siming lineage; reflecting on this once more, I [proceed].
The patriarch Baoyun and I, Siming, were like wise father and son, forming a complementary pair that revitalized this school during the Age of the Image.
Had their virtue and deeds not been transmitted to the world, the teaching would have lost its fundamental source; how then could later generations have investigated it?
Thus, I examined inscriptions and historical records, as well as various manuscripts, and obtained [the following].
The biographies of the Master and those who succeeded him thereafter comprise twenty chapters, compiled separately into one volume titled *The Collection for Reviving the Patriarchs of Baoyun*.
This title is taken from the plaque of the patriarchal hall of this monastery, which reads "Reviving the Patriarchs" (*Zhenzu*). Those who peruse these writings should understand this.
The beauty of the virtuous legacy left by my ancestors cannot be gathered up simply because I am a person of humble station and might otherwise be cast aside.
On a clear morning in the second month of the year Guihai of the Jiatai era, the Bhikṣu Zongxiao respectfully prefaces this catalog.

A Memorial to Request the Imperial Grant of a Plaque for the Ch’ŏnmunju Temple (The Monastic Subject) Sŏng Yen-de: Your servant, the monk Yen-de, having ventured to present his sincere devotion and thereby intruded upon Your Majesty’s celestial hearing, now reflects upon this transgression with deep trepidation and anxiety.
Your servant humbly recalls that his preceptor, the Upādhyāya, was a monk who transmitted the teachings of the Tiantai school.

The meaning [of this] applies to the monastery where he resided. In the first year of the Kaibō era, having received an application from Gu Chengwei, the former Transport Commissioner of Fuzhou, he entered the monastery to serve as abbot for the sake of the nation, providing long-term lectures on the Tiantai teachings.
With more than sixty disciples and over one hundred monastic quarters, he led the assembly in peaceful residence; although the provisions for the two daily meals were provided, [the text continues].

Ascending the lotus pedestal, you proclaim and extol the long-enduring imperial wind; yet while the splendor of the monastic community shines with brilliance, it has not yet received the honor of an imperial plaque.
We respectfully pray that Your Majesty the Emperor, responding to Heaven and sustaining the destiny of the realm, presides over the court with the observance of ritual propriety.

Thus, all nations are fully covered by your impartiality, and throughout the four seas, all sing of your sagely rule. This humble servant (the subject) has the fortune to encounter this sagely age and is privileged to participate in the True [Dharma].
I, your humble servant, venture to travel from afar to Your Majesty’s illustrious court, looking upward with hope for your gracious bestowal.

I beseech you to deign to turn your attention toward the construction project and graciously issue an imperial decree and command to grant my monastery its official title and seal. It is my earnest wish that this divine favor be manifestly conferred so that the Buddhist sanctuary may spread far and wide, illuminating the gateway of the Buddha-Dharma and forever assisting the transformation of peace and stability.
For having thus intruded upon Your Majesty’s august hearing, I am overcome with a sense of trepidation and gratitude. I, your servant, remain [in this state of] utmost humility.

Gazing toward Heaven, I am deeply grateful for Your Majesty’s sagacity; my feelings of extreme urgency and trepidation are beyond measure. I respectfully submit this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal and await Your Imperial Decree.
Dated the [blank] day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of Taiping Xingguo, this memorial is submitted by the monk Yan-de, a subject of the Mingzhou Chuanjiao Monastery.
Memorial Submitted.

Provincial Dispatch to the Secretariat and Chancellery: A dispatch concerning the request by the monk Yan-de of the Chuanjiao Monastery in Mingzhou for a change in the monastery’s name. Dispatch received:
By Imperial Decree, it is ordered that the Ministry of Personnel (Mingzhou) shall investigate the existing halls, corridors, merit-objects, and Buddha images currently housed within this monastery.

This document records the number of monks maintained and the dates on which [the images] were erected; it is issued for swift presentation to the Imperial Court. In accordance with the Imperial Decree, this notification is hereby issued.
Issued on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month of the sixth year of Taiping Xingguo.

A memorial from the Secretariat and the Chancellery to Mingzhou: Mingzhou has submitted a report stating that, in accordance with an imperial decree, they have inventoried the existing halls, pavilions, and corridors of the Chuanjiao Monastery, totaling over one hundred rooms; the Buddhist images number seventy; and the resident and visiting monks number fifty-eight.

It was established in the first year of the Kaibao era and reported to the throne. This memorial is issued in response to the decree: "It is hereby decreed that the name 'Baoyun Chan Monastery' shall be granted as its official title."
This notification is issued in accordance with the Imperial Decree.

The State Notification for the Chuanjiao Monastery: On the fifth day of this month, we have received an imperial edict in accordance with the memorial submitted by the Governor of Mingzhou.

By imperial decree, the monastery’s current buildings—consisting of over one hundred halls, pavilions, and corridors, along with seventy Buddha images and fifty-eight resident and visiting monks—were inspected and verified.

This monastery was established in the first year of the Kaibao era (968 CE). We hereby issue this notification in accordance with the imperial decree, which states: "It is fitting that the name 'Baoshou' be bestowed upon it."
The plaque inscribed with the name "Yun Chan-yuan" (Cloud Meditation Monastery) has been prepared as previously detailed and submitted to the Office of the Sangzheng for their knowledge and record.
This notice is hereby issued to the monastery itself, requiring that it comply with the instructions of the imperial decree.

In the spring of the Gengxu year of the Jianyan era, the monastery was reduced to ashes overnight due to the ravages of war. Among the charred remains, the stone inscription of the imperial edict bestowed by the Sacred Court was discovered;
its characters were so shattered and fragmented that they could no longer be deciphered. I have always lamented this with sorrow.
There was no longer any possibility of its being restored to its former state; yet twenty years after the *ji-si* year of the Shaoxing era, reaching the *geng-xu* year,
one day a monk from the Yao River suddenly brought this ink-cake, which (Zhongmin) received with joy as if he had obtained a precious treasure,
thinking that the lingering influence of his late ancestor, Dharma Master Tong, from his position in the teaching seat must surely still persist, so that it might once again flourish.
Fortunately, this was not so; how could such a coincidence be anything other than extraordinary? On the *wùzǐ* day of the first month of the following year, it was again incised upon stone.
Recorded by the former Superintendent of Monks within the jurisdiction, the presiding Abbot, Great Master Zhènjiào (Zhòngmín).
The *Siming Tujing* records the history of the Baoyun Jiaoyuan (Baoyun Teaching Monastery).
Located two li southwest of the county seat, it was originally known as the Chuanjiao Yuan (Teaching Transmission Monastery).

It was established in the first year of the Kaibao era of the Great Song Dynasty and renamed with its current title in the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era. It was originally donated by Gu Chenghui, the Regional Transport Commissioner.
The residence was designated for Master Yitong, whose teachings were transmitted to propagate the Dharma; he requested the name "Baoyun" (Precious Cloud) to manifest its auspicious significance.
Yitong, styled Weiyuan, was originally of the royal clan of Goryeo, having come from the Three Han states; his reputation resounded throughout China.

Zhi Li and Zun Shi were among his disciples, and his foremost senior students numbered more than two dozen. He passed away lying on his right side over twenty years ago; following his cremation, his disciples... [continued].
The remains were collected and enshrined on the southern slope of Mount Yùwáng; a stone stūpa was constructed by piling up rocks, and an inscription was recorded there.
The postscript was written by Wáng Bóxiáng, a *dàidìzhì* (Court Attendant for Literary Drafts), and both were carved upon the stone.
Biography of Dharma Master Jìngguāng of Luóxī in Tāizhōu (This biography appears in the *Dàsòng Sēngzhuàn*; it is now appended here for publication).
The Master’s name was Yiji (義寂), his courtesy name was Changzhao (常照), and he was surnamed Hu (胡). He was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou.
When his mother first became pregnant, she took no pleasure in meat or blood; at birth, the child had a purple cap covering his head.

In his youth, he petitioned his parents to leave secular life, and soon entered the Kaiyuan Hermitage (開元蘭若) to become a disciple and receive the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*). Day by day he mastered it, and the elders of the monastery...
The elders all sighed in admiration of his rarity. Subsequently, he shaved his head and received full ordination;

having gone to Kuaiji to study the Nanshan school, once he had mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka, he proceeded to Mount Tiantai to investigate and penetrate the *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. His ease of understanding was like that of the "Single Universal Radiance" (Yi-bian-zhao) in Henan.
Previously, the traces of the teachings of the Tiantai Master Zhiyi had been obscured by the distant destruction of An Lu-shan’s rebellion.

Consequently, following the destruction by fire during the Huichang era, with only fragmented manuscripts and broken scrolls remaining—where the branches were snapped and the transmission crushed—upon what could one rely to rectify one's studies?
The Master therefore constantly thought of collecting these fragments; while traveling through the ancient library of Jinhua, he obtained only the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Later, when King Zhongyi consulted National Teacher Deshao regarding the teachings and their characteristics (*jiaoxiang*), the Master instructed the Venerable One.

On this account, he memorialized the King requesting permission to go forth from the Golden Gate to establish a lecture hall; the King honored him with sincere devotion and had a monastery built for him, which is the present-day Luoxi Dinghui Monastery.

The King further dispatched ten men to the country of Japan to retrieve the Tiantai teachings, which were returned and bestowed upon the Master, who was posthumously titled Great Master Jingguang. The titles and names of the nine patriarchs were all established through the Master’s efforts.
In this way, the teachings of our single family have come to rely on masters as those who cause them to flourish;
Master Shao happened to share the same surname as Zhiyi, was able to assist and promote our school, and lived beside Fulong Mountain—therefore, I suspect he was his reincarnation.
Were it not for this master, how many students of this school would have taken a mere half-jewel to be their family treasure? (The fifth year of the Taiping Xingguo era).

From the mountains, he entered the capital city’s monastery and installed [the image] in the eastern tower. The tower was close to a great mountain, and one night he dreamed that the pillar of the *stūpa* (刹柱) sank into the ground;
he found this quite ominous. He moved it himself to a monk’s quarters on the western side. That night, the spring rain became torrential, the mountain collapsed, and the tower fell down.
Everyone said that the Master had foreseen this, proving that he had attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) as a karmic retribution. Subsequently, he received the yellow [robe].

The hermit of Yan invited [the Master] to board a boat and travel up the river to release living beings. They proceeded until they reached Haimen Lingshi Temple, the site of the Dharma-center where Zhiyi once resided.
Because he exhorted people to repair the temple and create statues, those who contributed funds were numerous.
At that time, the Emperor dispatched the high-ranking official Wei Shaoqin to enter the mountains to establish Shouchang Temple; various officials joined him in receiving the precepts there.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the Yongxi era, Dunqing of Yong’an County invited [the Master] to receive the precepts at Guangming Temple. Suddenly, from within the belly of a Buddha statue in the ancient hall, a vow-text was discovered.

It recorded that in the sixth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, the monk Xi Jiao had bestowed the precepts upon the people of seven villages and exhorted them to create this image, vowing:
"May I, upon the exhaustion of this retribution, be reborn as a male, remain in the state of a celibate youth, and always wear the coarse cotton robe of a renunciant."
The practitioner of the *Hōryū-kan* (Contemplation on Benefiting Beings through the Dharma) was the former incarnation of Eshi. In the tenth month of the fourth year [of Tenpyō], he fell ill;
on the fourth day of the first winter month, he instructed his disciples not to allow weeping or the performance of memorial offerings.

Having spoken thus, he closed his eyes and passed away at the age of sixty-nine and with fifty years of *dharma-lakṣa* (seniority). He had more than one hundred dharma-heir disciples, including ten monks from foreign lands.
In terms of his realization of the Dharma, he was a man of profound and lofty virtue; even those such as Fotudeng or Sengbao were but his peers.
At that time, the officials and commoners of the capital who had previously received the precepts from him all went together to Kaiyuan Temple to welcome the Master’s true likeness.

They made offerings with utmost sincerity, all wearing white mourning garments and weeping in grief, until the heavens themselves turned gloomy and somber. The Prefect Zheng Yuangui composed a poem in lamentation for his return to emptiness.

Fang Wen erected a stupa to commemorate him. Later, his disciples moved his remains to another location and opened the stupa; his countenance was as if alive, and his hair had grown more than an inch long.

During his lifetime, he had lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* along with its *Profound Meaning* (*Xuanyi*) twenty times each, as well as the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Brahmajāla*, the *Vajrasamādhi*, the *Dharmadhātudarśana*, the *Chan yuan quan*, and the *Yongjia ji*, each several times over. He also composed commentaries on them.
The *Yili*, *Buermen*, and other treatises comprise several fascicles. Yet, since the time of Zhizhe’s sixth-generation Dharma transmission down to Jingxi, more than two hundred years have passed;
how much more so for one who has received the late master’s entrustment and bears such a profound responsibility! Even during the sweltering summer months, he never perspires while lecturing.
Without having listened for long, his superior understanding of the Buddha Vehicle is such that whenever he proclaims it, [the audience is moved].

The sounding of the metal bells responded to the summoning of the jade chimes, as the *yu* and *shang* notes harmonized; for ninety days he discussed the subtle mysteries, yet how could one measure the distance between them?

Furthermore, while once staying at Yuwang Temple in Siming, he dreamed of ascending to the upper story of Guoqing Temple, where there was a precious, magnificently adorned bannered throne inscribed with the words "Mañjuśrī’s Platform.
Though he set up barriers and railings to block access, he had no means to enter. Suddenly, he beheld Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva emerging from the hall.
He slowly emerged and used his hand to push back the tethered horses; as the paths joined together for a moment, he felt himself and the body of Avalokiteśvara merge indistinguishably.
He then woke up with a start, and from that time forward, his joyful exposition has been inexhaustible.

Some say this was because he entered the wisdom of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), ascending to harmonize with the Buddha’s awakening by realizing the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment], and descending to harmonize with sentient beings by sharing the same essence as ordinary people.
When opened, the myriad spirits merge into a single Dharma; who else but Avalokiteśvara could have attained this mind? How great!
Such are the Master’s interpretations and practices—could they not serve as a model for the world?
Epitaph for the Stone Stupa of Dharma Master Tong of Baoyun Monastery in Mingzhou, Great Song, composed by the Dharma-grandson of Yanqing, the Grand Master Wenhui (Zongzheng).
The Dharma Master’s name was Yitong, his courtesy name was Weiyuan; his virtuous deeds are detailed in various biographies. He was a native of Haiguo, Goryeo.
His clan name was Yin and his mother’s surname was Shu. His birth was accompanied by many extraordinary signs, so he was placed in the Gui Shan Monastery.
When he reached the age of capping, he received the full precepts and studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*. He held these teachings in the highest esteem.

During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, while traveling extensively through China, he first visited Yunju where he attained awakening; subsequently, he went to visit Master Ji of Luoxi, through whom he fully realized the Tiantai school and its Way.
Furthermore, as the sound of his realization of the ultimate source spread far and wide, it was said that the study of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuandun) had reached its culmination here.
Desiring to guide those who had not yet heard this teaching, he set out from Shengdi, traveling eastward with his robes gathered in a sack;
his path led through Siming, where the Grand Master Qian Gong (Wei-zhi) questioned him on the essentials of the mind. Subsequently, he was appointed as a Precept Master and continued this Way.
The local people earnestly sought his presence, requesting him to remain as their refuge. The Master said, "This was not my original intention.
The official said, "Whether one is forbidden or encouraged, it is not within the power of a disciple. If you say it is for the benefit of living beings, why must it be only in Goryeo?

Since the conditions were such that he should comply, and the official did not refuse his request, the Master stayed there. Subsequently, the Regional Commissioner Gu Chenghui donated his residence to serve as a place for the transmission of the Way.
He requested the name "Precious Cloud" (Baoyun) to manifest its auspicious significance. Subsequently, he propagated the teachings and practices for over two years.
Zhi Li and Zun Shi were those whom he esteemed as superior; others who ascended to the Hall or entered his gate are beyond counting.
As for all his writings, they have mostly been lost and do not survive. Alas! The gentleman says: "The Way of Tiantai flourished once more through this Master."
He was sixty-two years old by secular reckoning. In the first year of the Duan-gong era, on the eighteenth day of the tenth month of the *wuzi* year of the Jiazi cycle, he manifested illness.
Three days later, he passed away reclining on his left side.

Following the rites, his disciples collected his remains and interred them at the northwest corner of the mountain to the east of Yuwang Mountain. Seventy-seven years later, they were re-encased in brickwork.
The site having become overgrown, it was cleared and a square mound was constructed there to further manifest its location.
On the tenth day of the late spring of the fourth year of the Jiaping era— the second year after the Heavenly King ascended the throne during the fifth reign of the Imperial Song,
the year being Jiachen— this record was inscribed by the Great-Dharma Grandson, [Zongzheng].

The above is the re-erected inscription for the stone stupa of Master Tong, composed on the twenty-first day of the tenth month in the year of Gengchen during the Shaoxing era by the Dharma-heir and Abbot Zhiqian.
Master Tong came from Samhan (Korea), where his reputation resounded throughout China;
he resided at Baoyun Monastery for over two decades, serving as its first-generation abbot in accordance with the Dharma. He was a true successor to Zhiyi, Zhili, and Ciyun.
That the teachings of the eminent Tiantai school, which had fallen into decline, were revived through the Master’s efforts,
and that the stone inscriptions concerning his life and deeds from that period no longer exist— Master Qian diligently searched for them until he first discovered the epitaph of the stupa,
which he then had re-engraved. Furthermore, he established the Zhen Hall, where he fashioned a seated statue of the Master, as well as [the image] of the King of Wuyue.

He composed a eulogy for the *uṣṇīṣa* image and erected a stone stele at the site of the Aśokarāja Mountain and Wushita Pagoda, replacing the wooden structures with stone to manifest this for future generations; thus, Master Tong’s Way became even more illustrious.

At that time, it had been barely more than half a year since Xianzhi arrived, and although Baoyun had personally begun the construction under Master Tong, after two hundred years of transmission, the buildings had recently fallen into ruin.
Qi was exceptionally humble; upon seeing this, [Zhao] was moved with deep emotion. He propped up the leaning structures and repaired the decayed parts, gradually restoring them to their former state.
This may indeed be called fulfilling the intent of the Founding Master’s entrustment to shoulder the burden.

During the Tianbao era of the Sacred Song dynasty, the Canal Commissioner Gu Chenghui donated his residence for the Master to dwell in. Later, Chen Yun, the District Magistrate, further donated the western [wing].
The island’s fields numbered four hundred and thirty mu, but after many years, they were no longer known;
Xian also fashioned statues of these two masters and set them forth, whereby people came to honor him all the more for his knowledge of the fundamental source.
It is said that Xian received the Dharma from Master Mingzhi, the fifth patriarch of Yanqing, and thus his own spiritual lineage likewise has its origin.
Written respectfully by Wang Boxiang, Left Court Dispersed Gentleman and Director of the Chongdao Abbey in Taizhou,
recording the relocation of the stupa of Dharma Master Tong of Baoyun Temple,
at Yuetai Hall on Mount Lingyin in Lin’an Prefecture. Composed by Daochang.
While I was residing at Yǔwáng Temple, Dharma Master Bǎoyún Wēi visited me and mentioned that Dharma Master Tōng was the patriarch who had initiated the teachings of Bǎoyún.
There was a stupa enshrined on this mountain; I inquired of the long-time residents, all of whom said it was located in the western corner of the temple.
I went there to search for it and found it amidst overgrown weeds and brambles—the stupa had already fallen into ruin. At that time, Wūshí...
There was a mountain that everyone said possessed excellent geomancy; several people of noble rank and wealthy families came to request it.
I considered that this land belonged to the monastic community and was not my private property; if I were to give it away myself, I would surely incur karmic retribution.
Although there were those among the local people who were deeply displeased, I alone maintained my resolve as before. At that time, our late teacher, the Venerable Miaozhan, resided at Xishan.
The pagoda was thus established based on what I received from my former teacher, who said that Master Tong was the patriarch of Tiantai.

Furthermore, the people of this region all desired to possess him; had the remains of Master Tong been moved and buried here, it would not only have prevented the incessant stream of those seeking land for burial, but also ensured that Master Tong’s bones were interred in their proper place. I therefore followed the counsel of my former teacher.
Following these words, they selected an auspicious day, and together with Master Wei and the elder Miaozhan, they assembled the multitude to relocate the burial.

Upon reaching it, they took the bones and washed them with scented water under the sunlight. What the world calls "hardened seeds" (*kaṭhina-bīja*) appeared—some green, some yellow, some red—or what was called "proliferating growths" emerged upon the bones. All who saw them were filled with joy, prostrated themselves, and offered praises.

This was a place of such excellence that it had never existed before in the world. Later, when King Houyu passed away, his disciples, recognizing the superiority of this site and wishing to secure its blessings, intended to enshrine him there. However, before long, everyone else’s remains were moved elsewhere;
only the stupa of Master Tong remained standing tall and solitary. Thus, one knows that the retribution for the goodness or lack thereof of one's mental application is manifest.

The efficacy [of this practice] is clearly visible. On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month in the twenty-eighth year of the Xiangxing era, the year Wuyin (1158), the monk Ruoquan of Yanqing visited me at Lengquan and presented the record of Master Tong’s reconstruction of the stone pagoda, seeking my calligraphy for the occasion of his reburial;
therefore, I have specially inscribed this for him. Thus it is said.
Written respectfully by the monk Dadaochang, residing at Yuet Tang on Mount Lingyin, recording the matter of the śarīra of Master Tong of Baoyun, Siming.
Master Tong of Baoyun was a native of Silla; having received the Dharma from Luoxi of Tiantai, he subsequently entered [China].
The reliquary stupa of the Extinguished Bone had been situated for many years to the left of the mountain gate of King Aśoka’s monastery.
Later, when the temple gates were relocated elsewhere, this site fell into ruin and the stupa likewise collapsed.

In the winter of the Dingwei year of the Xuanhua era, the present Chan Master Chang of Jiangshan presided over Yewang Monastery and moved the bone stupa to Mount Wushi; at that time, more than five hundred members of the assembly accompanied it.
Now, Chan Master Rui of Xuefeng and Dharma Master Wei of Baoyun were also among those present. Their bones were crystalline and lovely to behold;
when struck, they produced a resonant, clear sound. Xuefeng thought silently to himself that these must indeed be human bones, and that they would not stop at merely being like this.
A short while later, as the bright sun rose, he saw within the bones what the world calls "solid seeds" (*kaṭhina-bīja*).
Two or three members of the assembly were startled and began to clamor; in an instant, hundreds and thousands of brilliant, shimmering, and glistening objects appeared like pearls and jade beads.
Some people sought them out until they had filled their palms, yet those who obtained them remained silent.

I, [the author], recorded this in the Xinhai year of the Shaoxing era at Guangli Chan Monastery, and many have told me this story. Yet I still harbored doubts about it, until later I went to Wushi to pay my respects to Master Fayan.
In the master’s stūpa-hermitage, there was an old monk named So-and-so who could recount the matter exactly as it happened.
He further said, "I once requested two seeds and placed them in my palm; after grasping them for a short while, when I opened my hand to show them, they had already multiplied to seven or eight.
I then began to believe that this old monk was not a speaker of falsehoods. Furthermore, the Dharma Master possessed extraordinary features from birth. Formerly, during the Wu-Yue period...
The King held him in the highest esteem and once praised him, saying: "With the extraordinary mark of the white tuft and the wondrous form of the full moon, his fame spreads across a thousand *li*;
all gaze upon him with reverence. He also composed a poem which says: "Throughout my life I have relied on your compassionate eye; looking south, I sigh with deep admiration.

At that time, the Way of the Tiantai school had declined, but it was thanks to this Master that it was sustained. He transmitted the teachings to Fazhi and Ciyun, thereby establishing their respective houses.
This is what is called the lifeblood of the Tiantai school.

Regarding the traces of the writings of Master Jitong, the orthodox transmission of Tiantai ends with Chan Master Jingxi as the ninth-generation patriarch; however, as for the transmission following Jingxi...
This lineage has likewise remained unbroken; although they propagated both Samādhi and Prajñā, none could truly stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Nine Patriarchs.
Yet, in cutting the jade branches and splitting the sandalwood, all have practiced the Way of Tiantai.
Now, Master Tong of Baoyun truly succeeds Jingxi, and having received the Dharma from Fazhi and Ciyun, he has spread it throughout Jiangzhe, whereby this Way has once again been revitalized.
As for Master [Zhi]yi, his practice was profound and far-reaching, and his influence was vast and powerful.

Although the records of the Stone Pagoda state that his writings have all been lost and do not survive, an examination of the *Four Ming* commentaries reveals that he once took up the pen to compose works such as the *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, the *Record of the Profound Meaning*, and the *Subcommentary on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra*.
As for other doctrinal principles, Fazhi received them directly from him and recorded them in his own commentaries and sub-commentaries.
A single volume of his commentaries still exists, though it has not been widely circulated; what a pity!
The temple buildings established by the Master have stood for two hundred and twenty-two years, yet following the turmoil of war, ancient traces were swept away entirely.

I once informed the venerable elders that there was a pagoda containing the Master’s robes remaining at Jingqing Xingfa Monastery; they subsequently went to investigate and indeed enshrined them there.

Before the honored image in the Repentance Hall, there is a carved and embroidered canopy, exquisitely crafted and adorned with pure gold; it is hollow within and square without, standing approximately five feet high.
This precious object was an item from the Bao Yun Monastery; I know not by what cause it remained stranded in that temple.
Should this "pearl of Hepu" ever be returned, would it not serve as a banner for the preservation and transmission of our mountain school?
True Eulogy for Dharma Master Tonggong Baoyun By the King of Wuyue, Qian Chu Not departing from the three realms, he gave birth to our Great Master.
With the extraordinary mark of the white tuft and a wondrous countenance like the full moon, The pearl of his precepts shines everywhere;
the ocean of his wisdom is boundless. A gathering of blessings for humans and devas—behold him and look up to him in reverence!

Dharma Master Baoyun was the one who received the teachings from both the region of Ming and India; he was the patriarch who revived the traditions of *jiaoguan* (doctrinal study and contemplative practice).
Yet, as there were no sculpted images of him in antiquity, is this not nearly a forgetting of one’s roots?

Having established a seated image of him and further illustrated this original text, Zhiquan, together with the Prince of Qian’s eulogy, had them carved upon stone, so that those who gaze upon and pay homage may contemplate [his legacy].
As seen from the description of his appearance at that time.
Respectfully inscribed by the sixth-generation abbot and Dharma descendant, Great Master Yuancheng (Zhiquan),
in the sixth month of the early winter of the Gengchen year of the Xiangxing era.
A Poem Sent as a Gift to Dharma Master Tong of Baoyun Temple in Siming, by Qian Chu, King of Wuyue.
Beyond the sea and yet beyond the heavens, Our forms are parted, yet our Way is not distant. The lamp is green as I read the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*.
Fragrant and warm is the saffron robe upon his head; His precepts are like a flawless pearl. His mind is like a mirror from which all blemishes have been removed.
Relying on your compassionate gaze throughout my life, I gaze southward and sigh with deep emotion. (1)
Gazing at one another across several thousand li, we are distanced by a vast gulf from the Way’s intent. From this point on, our parting becomes final;
it seems as though we are separated for all eternity. Having attained the essential truth and explored profound stillness, I have no mind to compete for profit or fame.
In my thatched cottage on a clear autumn night, who will accompany me in chanting the sutras?
The second [entry] (by Zongxiao) records that while he was once perusing the *Ca'an Jiaoyuan Yishi* (Remnants of the Garden of Teachings from the Grass Hut), he encountered the so-called verse:
"Throughout my life I have relied on your compassionate gaze; looking south, I sigh with deep emotion. This was originally a gift sent by the Wuyue King Zhongyi to Baoyun Tong.
This is the work of the Dharma Master; it is a pity that we do not see it in its entirety, a regret I have harbored every day.
One day, visiting an old acquaintance, I obtained it and was overcome with joy. Even the jade of Jingzhou and the pearls of Sui would be insufficient to describe this;
indeed, it reveals how the ancients did not allow power or status to create barriers, but rather allowed their "Dharma-eye" to illuminate one another at the boundary between heaven and humanity.
This person was surely entrusted by the Buddha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; one served the world through loyalty and heroism, while the other propagated the Dharma through the power of his vows.
Although the worldly and the supramundane differ, their benefit reaching future generations without end follows the same principle (Zongxiao).
As a latecomer, I have fortunately been graced by the compassionate shade [of these masters]; how could I fail to record such great achievements of my ancestors?
Chuanjing respectfully records that these two verses he has presented have been engraved upon jade tablets to supplement the historical records of this mountain.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Festival of the year Renxu of the Jiatai era by the monk Shizhi (Zongxiao).
A Eulogy for the Fourth Patriarch of Baoyun in Mingzhou.
Preface by Shi Hao, Duke Wenhui of Kuaiji Prefecture.
The Master Zhizhe of Tiantai:

Pao-xi drew the *Yi* (Book of Changes), wherein the signs of the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) first appeared. With the alternation of Yin and Yang, they have already fallen into the realm of form and trace.
Gautama’s teaching of the Dharma causes body and mind to vanish into stillness; through the three cessations and three contemplations, the subtlest message suddenly leaks forth.
Within this, the ultimate mystery is profound, dark, and silent—what need is there for verbal expression? How could it be grasped through explanation?
Ah, how admirable is the wise one! Born with extraordinary brilliance, possessing eight-colored eyebrows and double pupils, such a person is truly beyond human comprehension.
Upon a single meeting with Nanyue, he suddenly clarified his past lives; He realized that the *śīla-dhāraṇī* was not obtained from another—how then could it be called "stopping and contemplating"?
Amidst the clamor and confusion, it was out of compassionate affinity And pity for the world’s delusions that he fashioned this expedient device.
It is like rescuing a sister-in-law drowning in water; How could one expect later students to seek it merely upon paper?
The written words are voluminous and profuse, yet the Way has become increasingly eroded and diminished. Only by penetrating the subtle meaning to the divine can one cast off the shell like a cicada;
though not departing from the place of ink and brush, this single seat on Vulture Peak is the Master’s fundamental vow.
Thus, the temple halls stand majestic and imposing, and his remaining countenance is extraordinary. Whenever any gentleman passes by, he must surely bow in reverence.

The Master Dharma of the School of *Samatha-vipaśyanā* by Bao Yun Tong: Flourishing in the Sui Dynasty, when the Dharma of the Final Age was not yet competitive and was on the verge of being submerged and forgotten, Master Tong rose up at the edge of the Three Han lands.
With his wind-sailed vessel crossing ten thousand *li*, he abandoned his raft to follow this teacher.

Having completed his attainment of the Way, he announced that the time for his return was near. The lay devotee of Siming, the Gu family, whose name was Chenghui, donated their residence to become a monastery.
With the utmost courtesy, they invited him to pray for blessings, naming it Baoyun (Jewel Cloud). The golden spire rose majestically;
once the Master had arrived, disciples followed like shadows. His door was filled with shoes, and his fame spread to the ends of the earth.
The lineage of Tiantai has fallen into decline; as the succession is re-established amidst rise and fall, there arise two of divine feet—true sons of the Lion King.
Ciyun and Fazhi harmonize with one another like the *xuan* and *chi* pipes. All people call them masters:

their brilliance and wonders coil and gestate, their roots planted firm and deep. They stand as a single trunk with solitary branches, blossoming into five petals; though their paths differ, they return to the same goal.
Up to the present day, Chan and the Exoteric teachings have thus been able to gallop side by side, continuing the life-span of the Buddha;
this is the legacy of our Master.
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Dharma-Wisdom Honored One of Siming, dragon-elephants gathered like clouds; the sheep, deer, and ox carts all returned together to the One Vehicle.
Raining down the supreme Dharma rain, universally moistening all sentient beings, reaching even into future generations;
Arising from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the sword of compassionate wisdom shatters the citadel of doubt. Who shall succeed him?
Ah, there stands the majestic lecture hall of Siming, profound in silence yet thunderous in its voice; The true lineage of Tiantai is here inherited.
When Emperor Zhangsheng was on the throne, he dispatched couriers as swift as stars to inquire about the great principles of the Buddha.

Having obtained their essence and refinement, imperial grace was bestowed once more, conferring upon him the grand title of "Dharma-Wisdom" (Fazhi). Thus, this son of the Śākya clan shall enjoy eternal glory throughout ten thousand ages.
—The Dharma Master Ciyun of India.
A brilliant and majestic master, a tiger among letters; pearls and jade at his lips, embroidery and brocade from his brush.
Honored by princes and nobles, favored by the Sage Ruler; the Compassionate Cloud bestowed his title.
In this land of India, Fazhi was his elder brother and Tonggong was his father; their eminent clan flourished like dragons leaping and phoenixes soaring.
Accumulating merit and piling up virtuous deeds, you have known the subtleties of cold and heat for ages. The fourfold assembly looks up to you with reverence, like children relying on their mother.
Your Brahma-sound resonates far and wide, pervading the entire universe; all liturgical texts and rituals are entirely derived from your compilation and arrangement.
Through the power of Samantabhadra’s vows, your golden hand strokes and comforts us, acting as the master of repentance throughout the bounds of the future.
The ancient site of Baoyun Monastery (Zongying) was inherited by this humble and unlearned person.
It happened that the Grand Tutor, the Chancellor, Duke of Wei, visited by imperial favor and first sought out the traces left by the Patriarchs.
Within a single shrine, amidst wind and rain, were the images of the two Great Beings, Zhiyi and Baoyun; they lay there in a state of decay. The Duke pointed toward Baoyun.
He turned to Zongying and said, "Did not the two venerable masters Fazhi and Ciyun arise from this very elder?
To this day, the people of this land regard it as the site of Master Tong’s practice hall; this was surely established for the sake of his two disciples.
One should open a hall there and sculpt or paint images of the four patriarchs to revitalize this monastery. Zongying was struck with deep shame and remorse.
The King and his ministers, with the intent of protecting the Dharma, immediately commissioned the construction of the Zhenzu Tang (Hall for Shaking the Ancestors) on the eastern corridor;

they established the images and ritual implements therein and invited Master Wei to compose eulogies. The Master did not fall into the trap of intellectual views nor engage in discursive thought, yet he composed four eulogies that were completed in a single sitting.
These works brilliantly elucidated the essential nature and physical form of our ancestors, providing a benefit for the observation and hearing of those throughout the four quarters.
(Zongying) having displayed it upon the plaque and further engraved it upon a solid stone, has thus restored the interrupted tradition of Baoyun as an inexhaustible legacy for our school.
On the first day of the fourth month in the fourteenth year of the Chunxi era, Zongying, the current abbot of Baoyun Jiaoyuan who transmits the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai,
respectfully inscribed this true eulogy for Master Tong of Baoyun.
Dwelling in the Mountain Hall of King Aśoka (Puzong), I bow my head.
The vast universe is opened like a window, revealing the true face of empty space; it cannot be gazed upon directly, so one may only look askance.
At once, flowers bloom upon the *udumbara*, and for ten thousand *li* the fragrance wafts from the *campaka*. With a discernment that cuts across the stream, he rolls up the ocean of learning.
He crossed the surging waves of the Dharma-eye and turned the twin wheels of the Heaven of Meaning; he beheld the nature of the Dharma-realm and entered the gate of Luoxi.

Thus we know that encountering the white ox is difficult to harness, yet applying the golden ointment makes it easy to clarify. He opened the secret bolt of the Three Contemplations and wielded the grand strategy of the mundane and the sacred.
How towering is his presence at the summit of the Mysterious Peak! His pure breeze from Huaihai stirs the vast expanse of space.
True Eulogy for Dharma Master Tonggong, the Founder of Baoyun Temple, composed by the Bhikṣu Kequan, who dwells at Zhuanan Hermitage on Nanhu: I bow my head and call out:
all people are my fellow villagers. Chanting through the clouds, sweeping away the lightning; from withered wood, spring is born.

By the power of his resolute vow, he has returned once more; I take refuge in the anniversary of the passing of Master Tong, the founder of Baoyun Temple and the successor to Tiantai. A draft of the memorial for the anniversary of the passing of Master Daoyin of Caotang.

On the right, I humbly submit: The Way is without past or present, yet learning has its lineages of transmission. A single drop branches into a thousand streams, yet a thousand carts share the same ruts. It is a matter of merit.
The merit of Great Revival is unsurpassed; one knows its source in the lineage of transmission. This extraordinary and orthodox teaching was widely propagated from master to disciple.
First, the legitimate heirs were esteemed: Fazhi and Ciyun appeared in succession, inspiring deep reverence.

One respectfully contemplates the Venerable Bao-yun, the great patriarch who upheld the teachings and contemplations, the true successor of the Tiantai lineage on Mount Yaowei, who is as present as if alive in his virtue, conduct, and physical form. I pay my respects.

The radiant light of Ling was divided into inexhaustible bright lamps and scattered as the boundless Dharma-rain; his physical form descended upon the maritime lands while his transformative traces flourished on the divine continent.
His true compassion concealed within a body of wondrous virtue, yet he manifested in response to the needs of the world like a dream or an illusion, appearing in the likeness of a bhikṣu.

His fragrant influence spread through Yong-shui, where the supreme teachings of his lineage shone once more in full splendor; the two characters of "Yin" and "Jiang" were proclaimed with great brilliance.
The extraordinary mark of the flaming white tuft has already been propagated through the *gāthās* in distant lands such as Kashgar; stupas compete to divide its *śrī* (merit).

We, [Name] and others, having humbly encountered this supreme transformation and beheld the likeness of his countenance, can do nothing but exert ourselves with longing, which only serves to increase our anxious distress.

Now that the season of early winter has arrived and the anniversary of his passing has come, we incline our hearts to prepare these offerings of pondweed and fern, though they are meager and insignificant.
I briefly extend this offering to honor those long departed; I humbly pray that my ancestors may partake of these offerings beyond all offerings, and manifest the ritual of coming and not-coming.

Relying upon these subtle and wondrous conditions, through the power of the breath of harmony and centrality, may the people be healthy and the things of the world abundant, seasons harmonious and harvests bountiful.
With the supreme flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta-maṇḍa*), may the spirits be nourished everywhere; with the Great Vehicle of the White Ox, may all people...
May the axle of human fatness be aligned so that the entire world may follow the same ruts; may all things, sentient and insentient alike, return to the Secret Treasury.
I, [Name], with utmost sincerity, prostrate myself and take refuge, and thus respectfully submit this memorial.
Memorial for the Anniversary of the Passing of the Honored Master Baoyun, Patriarch of Nanhu (by Jingshang Yixian):

We humbly submit that the source of the Dharma flows from afar, circulating throughout the ocean of lands; the sun of wisdom is now at its zenith, reflecting off the precious clouds below to adorn and illuminate the myriad capacities of beings.
As this sublime light shines forth, we dare not neglect the solemn occasion of his entry into extinction. May it be as we pray.
With the utmost reverence, we humbly observe that the Great Dharma Master Baoyun, an emanation body who appeared in Japan during the Zhongxing era, regarded all people as his own compatriots;
his great magnanimity transcended boundaries, and both of his eminent disciples possessed mastery over the true ground.
They clarified the orthodox lineage at Luoxi and dispersed the true wind throughout the world.

We, [Name] and others, look up to Your loftiness with ever-increasing reverence, yet we remain as if lost in bewilderment. As the jade desk bears the crossed scriptures, we regret not having been among the listeners at that time;
bowing beneath the *ni-tan*, we feel shame for our unworthy claim to be heirs to Your sagely plans today.

We humbly rely upon the permeation of Your clear faith and pray You will extend the mirror of Your compassionate pity. We beseech You: may the flame of non-arising wisdom eternally link with the radiance of the predecessors, and may it forever shine.

Residing at Miaohua-yi Can, where the later talents have reached their full potential and all students of the final age alike aspire to the Perfect Vehicle, I respectfully compose this sub-commentary.

(Formerly, when Meofeng had not yet been converted into a Chan monastery, Dahuang was a center for Tiantai teaching and contemplation. The Great Dharma-Eye Chan Master Qingliang also received the teachings there during that time. Baoyun Tong once attended his lectures, as did Siming Ciyun, both serving as members of the audience.
This account appears in the ancient inscription of Meofeng; the so-called Yufan Peak is the present-day Ayuwang Mountain).
The Dharma Master of Siming received his instruction from the Venerable Baoyun;
our ancestor Fazhi initiated the Great Teaching at the age of twenty when he went to study under Dharma Master Baoyun.
Only three days after he had entered the master’s gate, the Head of the Assembly said to him: "The Dharma-realm has its own natural order; if you seek it, you must follow the Teacher."
He asked, "What is meant by the 'Dharmadhātu Seat'? The Master replied, "It is this: the great totality of the Dharma-gate, perfectly interfused and unimpeded.

The student asked, "If it is perfectly interfused and unimpeded, how can there be any sequence? The student offered no reply. After one month had passed, he himself lectured on the *Heart Sūtra*, and everyone was struck with wonder at his exposition.
When the second year arrived, his father happened to dream that the Master was kneeling before Master Tong; Master Tong took hold of him...
Water from a jar poured into his mouth; he realized that this was the teaching and contemplation of his own school, and he attained sudden enlightenment.
Consequently, he took over the lectures for several years. Following the death of Daotong, he again dreamed of piercing Daotong’s head and wearing it upon his left arm as he walked.

He himself said that the first dream signified receiving and practicing the transmission, while the second signified upholding the seed-wisdom (*bījajñāna*). Thereafter, he moved to reside [at another location].
It was in the fourth year of the Qiánfú era that he finally accepted the invitation to Nán-hú.

The Master of Repentance Cíyún, who had studied under Bǎoyún and served as the Abbot of Cíyún Monastery, was a native of Níng-hǎi in Tái. He renounced his lay life at Dōngyè Mountain, and from the moment he became a monk...
Upon entering the country, he went before the statue of Samantabhadra at Guoqing Temple and vowed to study the sacred teachings of Tiantai by burning his finger.
Carrying his book-case, he proceeded toward Baoyun Monastery. On the way, he suddenly dreamed of a monk who said, "I am Master Mañjuśrī.

When he arrived and prostrated at the feet of Zhi Tong, he realized that the monk in his dream was none other than this master. Thereupon, he devoted himself to the teachings and received the Way under him.

Upon returning to seclusion, he went back to Tiantai. In the first year of the Chunhua era, when the Master was twenty-eight years old, the assembly invited him to reside at Baoyun Monastery for twelve years.
He lectured on the four great divisions of the sutras. In the fifth year of the Xianping era, he returned once more to Dongshan.

Later, he moved to Tianzhu, where he extensively propagated the Dharma and teachings until his final retirement there. There were four miraculous sites associated with the Master’s residence at Baoyun.
Once, while Master Yi was lecturing on a sutra at Baoyun Monastery, a mule from the Shi family suddenly approached and prostrated itself beneath his seat;
it departed once the lecture concluded. This occurred for a total of forty days until it gave birth and finally ceased coming.
That a mule could indeed possess human-like intent and be capable of listening to the Dharma—is this not extraordinary?

The two masters once established a Pure Land assembly at Baoyun Temple and authored a work titled *Record of the Vow to Be Born in the Western Land*, as well as a poem on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation (*Nianfo Sanmei*).
Its preface states: "The Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation is the wondrous path for realizing sainthood;

among all those who strive within the stream of the Dharma, who does not rely upon it? Formerly, when Master Huiyuan transformed the people of Xunyang, the multitude of worthies all became [his followers]."

Preface to the *Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation* by Yuan. During the Bingshen year of the Great Song dynasty, [Zunshi] gathered more than a hundred noble guests from Siming for two months, during the second months of spring and autumn, to assemble at Baoyun Lecture Hall for one day and one night of contemplation upon the immeasurable awakening and practice [of the Buddhas].

Since the sūtras of the Han and Wei periods were abolished in the Renyin year, I have long regretted that there was no record of this event at Mount Dongshan in Taizhou. Thus, I have composed these verses.
Thereupon, he modeled himself after Samantabhadra and composed a poem to be inscribed upon the stone for posterity.

While the three masters were residing at Baoyun Monastery, they were fortunate enough to receive the secret assistance of Avalokiteśvara; they commissioned artisans to create a sandalwood image of Mahākaruṇika.
When the image was completed, a craftsman made an error and broke off a hand holding a willow branch. The masters were struck with alarm and fear, whereupon they personally rejoined it themselves.
He applied glue so that it was joined together as before, and immediately composed a text of fourteen vows, the brief summary of which says:

"In the second year of the Xianping era, the year Jihai (999), on the fourth day of the fourth month, the śramaṇa Zunshe of Siming carved this image, fearing it might be obscured by later generations.
His own handwritten record states: 'Shen Jingyue carved the features; Zhang Jingxiu and others provided the materials for the image.'"
The image was established in the Great Dharma Hall, where one hundred monks were summoned to practice the sutras and dharmas to verify its efficacy.
In the third year of the Xianping era (990), Siming suffered a great drought; the people relied upon the Master to pray for rain.

The Master invoked the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara, making a solemn vow that if it did not rain within three days, he would immolate himself. When the time arrived, a great downpour indeed fell, and the Prefectural Governor... [honored him].
Su was struck by its uniqueness and revered it, immediately inscribing a record upon the stone.
The Dharma Master Mingzhi Baoyun, the incumbent, and Zhao Shuo (Shizhi) composed the "Record of the Master’s Conduct," stating: "The Master Mingzhong of Mingzhi was a native of Ningbo. Yuan...
Yū stayed at Enkyō for a short time before taking his leave; even the provincial governor could not detain him.
He said, "Wait until I am sixty years old, then I shall come again. From that time on, he lived in seclusion at Gakusan, and the assembly followed him there.
Later, when a vacancy occurred in a monastic office, the governor personally requested him to emerge and reside at Hōun-ji, which was indeed the path of his ancestral teacher, Dōkō.
At that time, the precious clouds [of the temple] were collapsing and ruined, with not a single rafter remaining intact. The Master rebuilt them, whereupon everyone said:

"The Master previously restored the residence of his third-generation ancestor; now he has again revitalized the hall of his fourth-generation ancestor. Who would say this is the age of the Final Dharma?
Previously, a prayer-text had been found within the belly of the monastery deity, which read: "A hundred years hence, there will be one of flesh..."
The Bodhisattva Shen rebuilt this site, but the Master again withdrew and built a hermitage on Mount Baiyun for four years;
there was not a single day during that time when he did not lecture. The Prefect then ordered him to reside at Yanqing, which he could not decline.
At that time, he was sixty years old, thus truly fulfilling his previous words (the *Ca'an Jiaoyuan Yushi* records that Mingzhi resided at Baoyun for eight years).
Petition for Master Ying to Reside at Baoyun Temple.
Your servant humbly submits this: In the past, the Great Disciple of Baoyun appeared like a fine steed emerging from the *wawa* pool;

having been perfumed by the correct views of Tiantai, he was like a fragrant orchid rising above the common mugwort and weeds. At a time when the world was becoming desolate and silent, he was like an A... [text fragment].

Regarding the difficulty of the Master’s transmission, we collectively reflect upon the newly appointed Dharma Teacher Baoyun Ying. Having received the mind-to-mind transmission, he is untainted by worldly burdens;

he has traveled extensively through the marketplaces of falling flowers and personally emerged from the furnace of smelting gold. With white hair and frost-like brows, he accepts the lay devotees’ entrustment for the year’s end;
morning incense and evening fires manifest the sincerity of the layperson’s "Flower-Covered" (Huafeng) blessing. Thus, he is one to whom all turn.
Respectfully drafted by Gong, who remains steadfast without regression.
Regarding the Record of the Benefit-Bringing Longevity Treasury of Baoyun Monastery:
When the Patriarch first arrived from Goryeo, he visited Luoxi and attained the Way of Tiantai in its entirety; thereafter, he desired to cross the sea [to China].
The Prefect, Lord Qian, firmly urged him to remain, and the Envoy, Lord Gu, also relinquished his own residence to serve as a place for the Master to transmit the Way and teach his disciples;
thus, the two great masters Fazhi and Ciyun emerged from this location.

Today, the site of Baoyun is what the local people call the "Dharma Site of Master Tong. Regarding the successive cycles of decline and restoration that occurred therein, they cannot be fully detailed.

In detail: when the abbot, Master Ying, had not yet been warmly settled in his temple, [the donor] first withdrew his headcloth and basin to appraise them among the assembly, obtaining one million coins;

both monastics and laypeople from within and without further obtained one million coins. Grand Preceptor, Duke of Wei, the Historian, donated the hairpins and earrings of the State Lady to provide for these offerings.
Combined, they formed the "Benefit for Long Life Treasury" (Lìyì Chángshēng Kù) to prepare for the seasonal requirements of construction, timber, and bells.

The drum had been struck for an indefinite period; five years later, a great lecture hall was constructed, and half of its dilapidated materials were taken to assist with the labor and construction—this was to fulfill his original aspiration.
Master Ying was pure and upright by nature and governed the assembly with leniency.

When Baoyun first returned, those with extravagant ambitions immediately raised disputes regarding status and hierarchy, and even some monastic officials relied on their authority to obstruct him, acting like tigers in power.
When bandits surrounded him, the people were struck with terror, yet Jing remained composed. The Grand Preceptor, Duke Wei, truly knew this; by this time, everyone was delighted and submissive.
I have heard that when the former Buddha sacrificed his body to seek the Way, there was not even a space the size of a mustard seed where there was no Buddha-body.

In the *shenxi* year of the Shaoxi era, Master Jing, the abbot of the mountain, constructed a Great Dharma Hall so vast and spacious that it was preeminent among all quarters.
At that time, Chan Master Tan of Zhuyuan visited this monastery and requested that it be given a name. The Master responded at once, saying:
"The name of the monastery shall be Baoyun (Precious Clouds). Clouds can bring forth rain, and rain can moisten all things; this monastery is the site where the Tiantai school was revived."
